title: The Illustrated Transformer
creator: Jay Alammar
summary: The diagram-led explanation of the Transformer that became standard reading in university courses. Alammar opens the model like a set of boxes: a translation black box, then an encoder and decoder stack, then a single encoder split into self-attention and a feed-forward layer. Self-attention is explained twice, once in plain words and once in matrices with queries, keys, and values, so the pictures and the equations finally agree.
headline: The Transformer, drawn one layer at a time
note: The matrices make sense on the second pass.

title: What Is ChatGPT Doing … and Why Does It Work?
creator: Stephen Wolfram
summary: Wolfram starts from a single question — what is the next word? — and keeps answering it until a language model has been built in front of you. Along the way he covers probabilities over text, what a neural net is, why training works at all, embeddings, attention, and where the whole thing stops being explainable. Long, but it assumes nothing, and the toy examples are runnable rather than decorative.
headline: What is ChatGPT actually doing?

title: The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Recurrent Neural Networks
creator: Andrej Karpathy
summary: Karpathy trains small recurrent networks on Shakespeare, Wikipedia markup, LaTeX, and Linux source, then shows what each one produces. The samples are funny, and they are also the argument: structure the model was never told about appears anyway. He follows with visualisations of individual neurons tracking quotes and bracket depth, which is the clearest early picture of a network learning representations nobody designed.
headline: Character by character, a network learns to write

title: Intro to Large Language Models
creator: Andrej Karpathy
summary: A one-hour talk that gets a general audience from tokens to fine-tuning without hand-waving. Karpathy frames a model as two files, walks through pretraining and the assistant training that follows, and then spends the second half on the security side: prompt injection, jailbreaks, and data poisoning. It is the talk to send someone who wants a real mental model rather than a metaphor.

title: Zoom In: An Introduction to Circuits
creator: Chris Olah, Nick Cammarata, Ludwig Schubert, Gabriel Goh, Michael Petrov, and Shan Carter
summary: The opening paper of the circuits programme argues that neural networks can be studied like cells under a microscope. Features are directions in activation space, circuits are the weighted connections between them, and both can be read off a trained vision model. Curve detectors and high-low frequency detectors are traced in detail. It is the founding document of mechanistic interpretability, and it stays concrete throughout.
headline: Looking inside a network, neuron by neuron

title: Core Views on AI Safety: When, Why, What, and How
creator: Anthropic
summary: Anthropic sets out why it works on systems it considers risky, and what it would do if the risk turned out to be high. The essay sorts possible worlds into optimistic, intermediate, and pessimistic, and describes portfolios of work for each. It also explains scaling laws as the reason safety research needs frontier models. A rare case of an organisation writing its reasoning down where it can be checked later.

title: Concrete Problems in AI Safety
creator: Dario Amodei, Chris Olah, Jacob Steinhardt, Paul Christiano, John Schulman, and Dan Mané
summary: The paper that moved AI safety from speculation to a research agenda. It names five concrete failures — negative side effects, reward hacking, scalable oversight, safe exploration, and robustness to distributional shift — and for each gives a small example, a set of possible approaches, and open questions. The cleaning robot examples are still the shortest way to explain why a well-specified objective can go badly wrong.
headline: Five accident risks, stated plainly

title: Intro to AI Safety, Remastered
creator: Robert Miles
summary: Eighteen minutes on why a capable system pursuing a slightly wrong objective is a problem, delivered without doom or hype. Miles builds the argument from specification, instrumental goals, and the gap between what we ask for and what we want, using examples simple enough to repeat to someone else afterwards. The best short introduction if you want the shape of the field before reading papers.

title: On the Dangers of Stochastic Parrots: Can Language Models Be Too Big?
creator: Emily M. Bender, Timnit Gebru, Angelina McMillan-Major, and Shmargaret Shmitchell
publication: FAccT '21 (ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency)
summary: The paper that named the stochastic parrot. It asks what scale actually buys, and totals the bill: environmental cost, training data too large to document, the way web text encodes the loudest voices, and the risk of fluent output that nobody meant. The argument is not that language models are useless, but that size is treated as progress while the costs stay unexamined.
headline: The costs hidden inside a very large model

title: ChatGPT Is a Blurry JPEG of the Web
creator: Ted Chiang
summary: Chiang's analogy is lossy compression: a language model stores a blurred copy of the web and reconstructs plausible detail when asked. From there he draws consequences — why models hallucinate confidently, why compression and understanding are related, and why writing with one may cost you the thinking that writing usually does. Short, precise, and the single best piece for a sceptical non-technical reader.
note: Worth arguing with, which is the point.

title: The Expanding Dark Forest and Generative AI
creator: Maggie Appleton
summary: Appleton takes the dark forest theory of the internet and asks what cheap generated text does to it. If anything can be produced at volume, proof of humanity becomes the scarce thing, and people retreat to smaller, quieter spaces. She sketches what remains legible: idiosyncrasy, specific detail, real reputation. Illustrated throughout, and unusually calm about a subject that normally invites panic.
headline: Where do you go when the web fills with generated text?

title: Why Chatbots Are Not the Future of Interfaces
creator: Amelia Wattenberger
summary: Wattenberger's objection is interface design, not capability. A blank chat box hides what the system can do, gives no affordances, and makes the user do the work of guessing. She shows alternatives — direct manipulation, visible controls, interfaces that suggest their own use — with demos rather than mockups. The clearest short argument that the text box is a default, not a destination.

title: Malleable software in the age of LLMs
creator: Geoffrey Litt
summary: Litt asks what happens to the old dream of software people can change when models can write code on request. He works through the difference between generating an app and giving someone durable control over one, and argues that the interesting layer is shared data with swappable tools on top. Grounded in his own prototypes, so the claims come with working examples.

title: Synthesizer for thought
creator: Linus Lee
summary: Lee draws the parallel with music synthesis: once sound became a space you could move through, instruments changed. He argues embeddings do the same for meaning, and sketches interfaces that let you blend, steer, and traverse ideas instead of typing prompts at them. Speculative, but backed by demos he built, and it gives you a vocabulary for what generative interfaces could be.
headline: Instruments for ideas, not just answers

title: A guide to prompting AI (for what it is worth)
creator: Ethan Mollick
summary: Mollick's practical position is that prompting is less of a discipline than it is sold as, and mostly comes down to context, examples, and iteration. He gives what works, what stopped working as models improved, and where the popular tricks are cargo cult. Useful because it is written by someone who tests claims with students rather than collecting them from social media.

title: Catching up on the weird world of LLMs
creator: Simon Willison
summary: Willison's catch-up talk covers how the current models arrived, what they are genuinely good at, and the failure modes that keep biting people in production. He is specific about prompt injection, about evaluation being harder than it looks, and about the gap between demo and system. A good calibration pass if you have been following the news but not the substance.
headline: A field update, delivered without hype

title: Demis Hassabis — Scaling, superhuman AIs, AlphaZero atop LLMs, AlphaFold
creator: Dwarkesh Patel and Demis Hassabis
summary: The head of Google DeepMind on why scaling is still, in his words, an art form rather than an engineering discipline, and on what happens when you put AlphaZero-style search and planning on top of a language model. Patel presses him on timelines, on whether an intelligence explosion is a thing you can steer, on keeping model weights out of the hands of states that want them, and on how Gemini was actually trained. A transcript is posted alongside if you would rather read it.
headline: Search, planning, and the limits of scaling

title: Beth Barnes on the most important graph in AI right now
creator: Rob Wiblin and Beth Barnes
summary: METR times how long a task takes a skilled human, then measures which of those tasks models can finish. The resulting number — the length of job a model completes half the time — has been doubling roughly every seven months, which is the graph of the title. Barnes explains how the measurement is built, why chain-of-thought being readable is a safety property worth protecting, and what alignment faking looks like in practice. Very long; the timestamped outline and full transcript let you take it in pieces.
headline: The seven-month doubling, and how it is measured

title: But what is a neural network? | Deep learning chapter 1
creator: Grant Sanderson
summary: Sanderson builds up a network that reads handwritten digits from a 28x28 grid, one layer at a time, and insists on the question most explanations skip: what could an individual neuron plausibly be detecting, and why does stacking those detections help? Weights, biases and the sigmoid arrive as answers to that question rather than as definitions, and the animation carries the linear algebra without hiding it. Training comes in the next chapter; this one is about what the object actually is.
headline: What the layers are actually doing
